---
title: Playground execution image
description: Build and qualify the shared eleven-language Linux image for hosted Playground.
---

## Build and qualify the exact image

Build the image in CI, never on a workstation. Dispatch the
`Playground execution image` workflow (`playground-execution-image.yaml`) on
`main` at the reviewed commit. It holds no Cloudflare credentials. The job
builds the Dockerfile in `apps/playground-execution/container` for
`linux/amd64` and then runs two qualifications:

- `verify-image.mjs` runs every stock template under Docker's own isolation.
- `qualify-launcher.mjs` runs the real launcher (`run.py`) as the slot does,
  with only the capabilities it needs to build its sandbox. It checks every
  stock template; UID, GID, capability sets and no-new-privileges; denied
  egress to public, metadata and private addresses and DNS on a bridged
  network, so the launcher's network namespace is the barrier; writes outside
  the workspace; the command timeout; the output limit; and the process limit.

The job uploads `image.tar.gz` and `receipt.json` (source SHA, image ID, tag, image and archive sizes,
archive SHA-256, run ID) as the `playground-execution-image-<sha>` artifact for
14 days. The registry upload is a separately approved operation on that
archive.

## Upload the image to the registry

Dispatch `Playground execution registry upload`
(`playground-execution-registry.yaml`) on `main` with the image run ID and its
full source SHA. The job accepts only a successful image run of that commit on
`main`. It verifies the archive SHA-256 and image ID against the receipt, then
pushes with the lockfile-pinned `cf containers push --tag`, retrying a failed
push at most three times. It checks out the dispatched `main` tip, and the image
commit must be an ancestor of it. It runs in the reviewer-gated `playground-registry` environment. Its
only credential is the environment secret
`PLAYGROUND_REGISTRY_CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`: a short-lived token scoped to the
Tuturuuu account and Containers registry write. The account comes from the
`CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` variable. The job uploads a receipt with the registry
reference `registry.cloudflare.com/<account>/tuturuuu-playground@sha256:<digest>`
that the Worker image configuration uses. Revoke the token after the upload.

The fixture uses the same stock commands that Meet and Learn load. It checks
Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C, C++, Java, Rust, Go, Ruby, PHP, and Shell.
Each template runs in a fresh local container with UID and GID 65534, all
capabilities removed, no new privileges, no network, a read-only root, and
bounded writable directories. The Dockerfile uses a pinned amd64 base manifest and signed, dated Debian
snapshots. Refresh the base and snapshots together when updating toolchains.
The image contains no application credentials.

Record the source SHA, build invocation, result for every language, and image
ID. After an approved registry upload, also record the Cloudflare registry
digest. Use the digest in the Worker image configuration. The local image ID
and the registry manifest digest identify different objects. Retain the
previous digest while it is a rollback target. [Cloudflare image management](https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/guides/image-management/)

## Deploy to staging and qualify the sandbox

Dispatch `Playground execution staging deploy`
(`playground-execution-deploy.yaml`) on `main` with a registry reference
pinned by digest. The build job has no credentials: it runs the Worker tests,
builds the staging Worker with `cf build` (driven by the app's
`vite.config.ts` and `@cloudflare/vite-plugin`), and checks that the emitted
output names only that image and every Durable Object class. The deploy job
runs in the reviewer-gated `playground-staging` environment. It deploys the
prebuilt output with `cf deploy --prebuilt --no-provision`, uploading the
ingress and operator secrets from the environment through a temporary
secrets file, then runs hosted qualification and confirms admission is still
paused. The environment holds `PLAYGROUND_STAGING_CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` (a
short-lived token minted for the run), `PLAYGROUND_STAGING_INGRESS_SECRET`
and `PLAYGROUND_STAGING_OPERATOR_SECRET`, and uses the `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`
variable.

Staging is reachable only on its `workers.dev` hostname, so it needs no zone
or route change. Only the staging configuration contains the qualifier: the
`PLAYGROUND_QUALIFY` flag, the `PLAYGROUND_QUALIFIER` binding and its one-guest
container class. Staging builds from `src/staging-worker.ts`, which adds the
qualifier class and the `/qualify` route to the production entry
`src/worker.ts`; production builds from `src/worker.ts`, so neither reaches
its bundle. A configuration test, a bundle test and the production build's
shape check enforce this, and `/qualify` in production answers like any
unknown path. Workflow checks that something is absent use
`if grep …; then exit 1; fi`: Bash ignores `set -e` for a negated `! grep`
that is not a step's last command, which `workflow-negated-commands.test.js`
refuses.

`POST /qualify` takes the operator secret. It starts one fresh guest and runs
fixed fixture jobs, never request input, through the production exec,
launcher and sandbox. The cases are every stock template, standard input, the
dropped identity and capability sets, denied egress to public, metadata and
private addresses and DNS, workspace write bounds, the command timeout, the
output and process limits, and a compile-only check per language. It also
records the guest's own view as root (identity, capabilities, kernel version)
and tries each sandbox layer on its own: the security modules, the `/tmp`
tmpfs mount, the namespaces, the identity drop, Landlock, and the launcher's
full preflight chain. Each line reports its exit code and error, so a runtime
that refuses one layer is named rather than failing every case with
`sandbox_failed`. The report also has the cold start time; the guest is then
destroyed. The job uploads the report as `playground-execution-qualification-<sha>`
and fails unless every case passed and the guest stopped. Check cases need an
image built from a commit that includes check mode.

## Two-participant acceptance on staging

Dispatch `Playground execution staging acceptance`
(`playground-execution-staging-acceptance.yaml`) after a staging deploy. In the
`playground-staging` environment it opens staging admission, then for every
language one participant Runs the stock template through `/run` and
`/result`, the other reads that Run, and they swap. Admission is paused again
whatever the outcome (a final step pauses it even when the run is cancelled), and the report (`playground-execution-staging-acceptance-<run>`)
records each Run's status, output and duration.

Staging has no Web project to load source from, so the Runs carry a signed
fixture source ticket (`src/fixture-source.ts`): HMAC-SHA-256 over the
project, revision, language and an expiry of at most 15 minutes, keyed by a
key derived from the ingress secret for fixture tickets only. The slot accepts it only where `PLAYGROUND_QUALIFY` is
enabled, which production never sets, serves only the named stock template
and skips the writeback. Everything else is the production path: ingress
authentication, admission and per-person limits, slot assignment, a fresh
guest, results and stop. The Web source hop is covered by the production
Meet-room test, under a short admission window, before Meet turns the cloud
Run adapter on by default.

## Deploy to production

Dispatch `Playground execution production deploy`
(`playground-execution-production.yaml`) on `main` with the registry
reference staging qualified. The credential-free build job pins the source
origin to `https://tuturuuu.com` (Web production, which serves
`/api/v1/internal/playground-execution/source` and `/export`) in the workflow,
like the ingress host: a job that binds no environment reads an
environment's variables as empty, which `workflow-environment-scope.test.js`
refuses for any name carrying an environment's prefix. It checks that the emitted output names only that digest, the custom domain
`playground-execution.tuturuuu.com` and the source origin, with no qualifier
class and no staging name. The deploy job runs in the reviewer-gated
`playground-production` environment with `PLAYGROUND_PRODUCTION_CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`,
`PLAYGROUND_PRODUCTION_INGRESS_SECRET` and `PLAYGROUND_PRODUCTION_OPERATOR_SECRET`.
`cf deploy --prebuilt --no-provision` attaches the custom domain on the
`tuturuuu.com` zone, so the token also needs that zone's Workers route
permission.

The environment's reviewer
confirms the digest passed staging qualification before approving. The
admission gate is durable: it starts paused, and when the domain already
serves the Worker the job pauses admission before rolling out containers.
The smoke waits for the custom domain to
serve the Worker, then requires an unauthenticated `/run` to answer 401 and
`/qualify` and `/` to answer 404, and pauses admission again through
`/control`. Enabling admission and turning on Meet's cloud Run adapter are
separate operator steps after the smoke.

Web reaches the Worker through `PLAYGROUND_EXECUTION_ORIGIN`
(`https://playground-execution.tuturuuu.com`), sends the same value as
`PLAYGROUND_PRODUCTION_INGRESS_SECRET` as `PLAYGROUND_INGRESS_SECRET`, and
signs source and export tickets with its own `PLAYGROUND_SOURCE_TICKET_SECRET`.
Roll back by pausing admission, then removing the custom domain from the
Worker; the Worker keeps the previous digest's deployment for
`cf`-based rollback.

## Hosted qualification

Run the fixture again against the digest on the actual Cloudflare execution
path before enabling product traffic. Prove the guest has no external DNS,
direct IP, or private network egress. Check effective UID and GID, all Linux
capability sets, no new privileges, filesystem write bounds, resource limits,
command timeout, output truncation, cancellation, and descendant cleanup.
Confirm the container stops after idle. Measure cold latency and, if the
per-run isolation boundary supports reuse, measure warm latency with a clean
workspace. Include a second participant's result from a real Meet room for
each language.

A Docker fixture verifies the image and template contracts. Cloudflare applies
its own runtime policy. In particular, Durable Object scheduling does not
remove root capabilities merely because an exec process sets a numeric user.
Require hosted isolation evidence before enabling an execution route. [Cloudflare Container exec](https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/api/durable-object-container/#exec)

## Cloudflare admission and rollback

The Cloudflare path uses a dedicated Worker, a SQLite coordination Durable
Object, and at most 20 slot Durable Objects that can start guests. Meet keeps
its existing authorization and passes a short-lived capability for the exact
saved revision. The slot uses that capability to download source from Web.
The source-signing key stays in the application servers. The guest receives
only the saved files, command, and stdin.

The Meet adapter is selected only when
`MEET_PLAYGROUND_EXECUTION_PROVIDER=cloudflare`. The Durable Object starts
with admission paused. The ingress and operator secrets are separate.
Production deployment, registry upload, secret installation and
admission changes each require operator authorization for the exact operation.

| Configuration | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `PLAYGROUND_MAX_CONCURRENT` | 20 active slots |
| `PLAYGROUND_MAX_CONCURRENT_PER_USER` | 1 active Run per requester |
| `PLAYGROUND_MAX_RUNS_PER_USER_10_MINUTES` | 30 starts per requester in a rolling 10-minute window |
| `PLAYGROUND_MAX_STARTS_PER_UTC_DAY` | 5,000 starts per UTC day |

Set the values lower for an early deployment. The defaults are also the approved
ceilings. A duplicate request uses the original receipt and consumes no further
start allowance. A failed or ambiguous dispatch consumes its original allowance.
The active project limit protects shared rooms where two participants can ask to
run the same revision. The current Meet adapter handles Run, Stop and Console
results. File changes use the existing collaborative merge and revision-checked
Drive checkpoint. Preview and Learn retain their current provider. Qualify the
writeback and concurrent editor behavior before production activation. Verify
that the legacy runner pool has no eligible Playground capacity while Meet uses
Cloudflare and Learn still uses the legacy provider.
The legacy readiness probe requires `python3` and the language toolchain.
For Java, both the `javac` compiler and the `java` launcher must be on PATH.

The operator calls `POST /control` with the operator credential and
`{"enabled":false}`. The response records the new generation and the number of
active reservations. Admission then refuses new work. A draining response uses
HTTP 202. A claimed Drive writeback keeps the reservation active until the
coordinator receives the checkpoint confirmation, or until 60 seconds after the
job deadline. That grace covers one room checkpoint and its settlement calls;
after it the Run fails without a saved revision and releases its slot, user and
project, so a lost settlement cannot wedge capacity or block re-enabling. Stop fences new writes
and lets an in-flight export finish its bounded receipt wait. Confirm there are zero
active reservations and zero running instances before rolling back the
application route or rotating service secrets. The same control request is
idempotent. Re-enable only after a scoped approval and verified teardown.
Keep the result endpoint available for existing cloud run receipts while
switching the Meet adapter back to its previous provider.

An accepted reservation schedules finite work. The normal path makes one
assignment RPC, one source fetch with an eight-second timeout, one guest
start, one command, one finalization, and at most one file export. The slot journals its start before
fetching source. Interrupted execution is reconciled without launching the
command again. Cleanup makes at most three attempts per reservation. If
cleanup stays unconfirmed, the slot remains occupied for operator
reconciliation. Clients stop polling at the run deadline. Terminal jobs clear their deadline work. Result polling
uses only the journal. A new admission prunes up to 64 expired receipts.

The Node tests in `apps/playground-execution/src` pin these counts.
`admission.test.mjs` covers the ledger: statements per reservation, restart
deduplication, daily and rolling limits, the pause fence and the cleanup
budget. `slot.test.mjs` covers the slot: the normal path's fetch, start,
command and storage writes, no replay after a restart in the started phase,
an unconfirmed teardown that keeps the slot occupied, and Stop or pause before
the guest starts. `container-run.test.mjs` covers the guest: egress disabled,
output bounds and confirmed destruction. Run them with
`bun run --cwd apps/playground-execution test`.

## Code checks

`POST /check` returns compile-only diagnostics for unsaved room files in C,
C++ and Java. No program runs. The coordinator charges a separate check
budget in its own table: 60 checks per requester and 300 per room in a
rolling 10 minutes, and `PLAYGROUND_MAX_CHECKS_PER_UTC_DAY` (default and
ceiling 20,000) per UTC day. Every attempt is charged, including a retry
with the same request ID, and an ID already used by another person or room
is refused. The durable admission gate that pauses Runs pauses checks too,
and a pause also stops the warm guests of rooms with checks in the last 35
minutes; `/control` answers 202 until each confirms it stopped. The pause is a
durable fence: a check admitted before it is refused even if it reaches the
room's checker afterwards.

Each room with recent checks has one `PlaygroundChecker` Durable Object and
one warm guest on the `basic` instance (1/4 vCPU, 1 GiB) with Internet
disabled. The guest stops after 90 seconds without checks, and an alarm
replaces it 30 minutes after it starts, even under continuous checks. Check
admission caps the rooms checked within the last two minutes, and therefore
the live guests, at 50, and at three per person. A new room past a cap gets
`check_quota` with a retry for when the oldest counted room's guest idles out. Durable Object containers take their instance type at
`start()` and no instance count from `cloudflare.config.ts`, which `cf build`
rejects for them, so the code enforces every guest bound. A cold room starts its guest and answers `check_warming`; the client
retries. Each person has at most one check in flight, and a newer check kills
the older one (`check_superseded`). A room runs at most two checks at once
(`check_busy`).

Every check is a separate exec with its own mount namespace, a fresh `/tmp`
workspace, PID and network namespaces, the dropped identity and the write
bound below, so
nothing a check writes survives it or reaches another check. The launcher
runs a fixed command, never one from the request: `gcc` or `g++` with
`-fsyntax-only`, or `javac -proc:none -implicit:none` with a throwaway class
directory. Sources are passed as `./path` so no file name is read as an
option or argument file. gcc and g++ get 4 seconds of wall and CPU time
and 512 MiB of address space; javac gets 8 seconds, because a cold JVM on the
smallest instance needs more, and a 192 MiB heap. The Worker abandons a check
4 seconds after the guest's own limit, and the sandbox dies with its
launcher, so a killed or superseded check leaves no compiler running.

The Worker reports diagnostics only for request paths; a problem located in
any other file (a toolchain header or an absolute include) becomes the fixed
text "Problem in an included file" at the include site. A message located in
a request file can still quote a value the compiler derived from an included
file, and an include can test whether a path exists. The guest holds only the
public image and the request's own files, so this reveals nothing a Run could
not read.

A warm room guest costs about $0.00000278 per live second plus the CPU of
its checks, about $0.012 per active room-hour at the published overage rates.

## Launcher behaviour

The trusted launcher (`container/run.py`) runs as root only to mount a fresh
`/tmp` and build the sandbox. In its private mount namespace it then
replaces `/dev` with a tmpfs holding only bind mounts of `null`, `zero`,
`full`, `random` and `urandom` (no device node is created) and the
`fd`/`std*` links, remounts every mount except `/tmp` and
`/proc` read-only, keeping each mount's `nosuid`, `nodev`, `noexec`,
`nosymfollow` and atime flags, and checks that no reachable mount is left
writable. The program has no capabilities, so it cannot remount them: the
read-only mounts are the write bound. Landlock (writes only beneath `/tmp`
and to `/dev/null`) is layered on top when the kernel implements it. The
Cloudflare microVM kernel does not (`landlock_create_ruleset` returns
`ENOSYS`), so hosted guests rely on the read-only mounts alone; the hosted
qualifier's layer probe reports which applies, and `qualify-launcher.mjs`
runs the write-bound case both with Landlock and under a seccomp profile
that makes its syscalls return `ENOSYS`, asserting the fallback really ran
and that a user namespace cannot make the mounts writable again. Without
Landlock the program can still write to `zero`, `full` and the random
devices (harmless). `/proc` is read-only too: the launcher re-enters itself
as PID 1 of the program's namespaces, mounts that namespace's `/proc`
read-only with `nosuid`, `nodev` and `noexec`, and only then execs the
privilege drop, so the program cannot write its own `/proc/self` tunables
(`comm`, `oom_score_adj`, `attr`) and cannot mount a writable `/proc` from a
user namespace. Go's standard library is compiled into the image
(`/usr/local/lib/playground/go-cache`), and each Run gets a writable overlay of
it at `GOCACHE` whose upper layer lives on the workspace tmpfs, so `go run`
links instead of building the standard library, which takes longer than the
30-second command timeout on the smallest guests. The hosted chain probe
reports whether that overlay mounted (`gocache True`). Landlock is used only
from ABI 3, the first with every right
the rules need. The launcher then runs the same
namespace and privilege-drop chain around `/bin/true`. If any stage fails,
the Run is `sandbox_failed` before user code runs, and its output names only
the stage (`input`, `workspace`, `devices`, `confinement`, `landlock`,
`preflight` or `command`). The
program then runs as UID and GID 65534 with no capabilities, no new
privileges, an empty network namespace, its own PID namespace and writes limited to
`/tmp`.

After a normal exit the launcher exports the workspace as a complete
inventory. Files the program created that cannot be saved (binaries, names
outside the path rules, files over 256 KiB, non-UTF-8 text) are left out. If a
project file still exists but cannot be saved, or the workspace exceeds the
inventory or size limits, the launcher returns `files: null`. The slot skips
Drive writeback and preserves the program's exit code, output and outcome.
An empty array is a complete inventory and can record file deletions.

## Logs and first-Run telemetry

The Worker has Worker logs on and per-invocation request logs off, so the
volume stays bounded. Two events carry only identifiers, an outcome and
timings. No user, project, file, command, input or output value is ever logged.

| Event | Where | Fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `playground.run.accepted` | `/run`, on admission | `runId`, `colo` |
| `playground.run.guest` | the slot, once per guest attempt | `runId`, `slot`, `guestMs`, `outcome`, `firstInIsolate` |

- `colo` is the Cloudflare data centre that took the `/run` request. `/run` is
  a server-to-server call from Web or Meet, so this is the data centre nearest
  that caller's egress, not the participant and not where the slot or container
  runs.
- `guestMs` runs from the guest start through teardown. It includes setting the
  inactivity timeout, the coordinator's execution check, reading and parsing the
  output and destroying the container. It excludes the source fetch and any
  isolate start-up before it.
- `outcome` is the guest's `exited`, `timeout`, `output_limit` or
  `sandbox_failed`. When the guest produced no result it is `stopped` (a Stop
  arrived) or `error` (the Worker deadline, a launcher fault, a malformed
  response, a refusal while the guest is starting or an unconfirmed teardown).
- `firstInIsolate` is true for the first guest this Worker isolate starts, as a
  rough proxy for a cold start. Every Run still starts a fresh container.

Join the two events on `runId` to compare `guestMs` for first and later Runs
against the first-Run latency users see. A Run that stops before a guest
attempt (source fetch, claim, or a refusal before the guest attempt starts)
logs no `playground.run.guest` event.

## Image size baseline

The shared image measured 1,672,640,086 bytes (about 1.67 GB, image run
45378869075). The largest contributors:

| Path | Size |
| --- | ---: |
| `x86_64-linux-gnu` libraries | 439 MB |
| `jvm` | 287 MB |
| Rust `rustlib` | 172 MB |
| `share/go` | 170 MB |
| `lib/go` | 113 MB |
| `local/bin` (Bun) | 103 MB |
| `libexec/gcc` | 101 MB |

Slimming the image is parked. If first-Run telemetry shows start latency is a
problem, dropping Bun is the first option to evaluate, then the toolchains
that the stock templates need least. Qualify any slimmer image with the same
fixture and staging gates before it is used.

## Usage and cost

The initial instance size is 0.5 vCPU, 4 GiB of memory, and an 8 GB disk.
The command has a 30-second timeout within a 50-second job deadline. Output
is capped at 64 KiB. Fresh instances are destroyed after execution, with a
15-second inactivity timeout as a fallback. Warm reuse requires independent
hosted qualification before use.

At published overage rates, the estimated Containers cost is
`$0.00001056 × live seconds + $0.000020 × active vCPU-seconds`.

| Modeled Run | Live seconds | Active vCPU-seconds | Cost per Run | Cost at 150,000 Runs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Cold | 45 | 5 | $0.0005752 | $86.28 |
| Warm, conditional | 25 | 2.5 | $0.0003140 | $47.10 |
| Stress scenario | 70 | 35 | $0.0014392 | $215.88 |

A 15-second idle tail costs about $0.0001584 per instance plus actual CPU.
Sleeping container compute is $0. The estimates exclude the Workers Paid
base charge, Workers and Durable Object requests, duration, SQLite storage,
and logs, and are before shared included allowances. The stress scenario
is an estimate. Provider shutdown latency can change billed usage. Record
real cold-start and shutdown times, journal operation counts, and actual
usage during qualification. [Cloudflare Containers pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform/pricing/) · [Workers and Durable Objects pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/)
